job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Vera Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Vera. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live at home in Ashby Cross with my parents. Dad is the caretaker at St Brigid's church and Mum is a school cook, so the house is up early. I take the 7:40 bus to Hallam University, fifty minutes each way, for my master's in information systems. On the bus I read my notes on paper, because the screen gives me a headache. Evenings I help at the church youth club, and Thursdays I clean the hall with Dad.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science, with networks as my main subject. A pass, not a good one. My final project was setting up a secure network for a small parish office, and they still use it. I didn't do an internship, because the firms that offered them were two hours away and I couldn't afford the rent. I owe about thirty-two thousand, and my parents have nothing to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said: tools come and go, and good work is still good work. I'd tell the youth club kids that a machine can't be honest or kind for you. I wouldn't be too bothered, because I've seen a lot of things called the future that weren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing has changed, and that's the trouble. There are two or three firms near me that hire in IT, and they take people with a better degree or a contact. I've sent out about fifty applications and had four replies. It's my debt and my pass that hold me back, not a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep helping at the church, and ask every person I know if they've heard of work. I'd go to the local business breakfast that the parish priest recommended and shake hands with people. I'd apply to the council and the hospital, because public jobs are stable. And I'd stay away from AI tools. I like to understand every step of what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired but patient. My faith helps, but it doesn't pay the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've had four replies in fifty. What did they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two said thank you, no. One invited me for a call and wanted someone with experience in a tool I'd never used. One said they'd keep my details. I print each reply and put it in a folder, which is probably silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus pass, which means I'd cycle part of the way. Then I'd stop buying books and use the library. I'd never cut the youth club or what I give at church, though, because those are what hold me up.

I'd tell the youth club kids a machine can't be honest or kind for you.
think: Nothing has changed: only two or three local firms hire in IT, and they want a **better degree** or a contact.

Keep running the church youth club and Thursday hall cleaning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful, because a lot of firms will use it to cut people and call it progress. I'd say that anyone who wants a job should learn a skill that needs hands or trust. I'd say it quietly at church and more firmly to my cousin who works in a call centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the first jobs to go are the ones I'm applying for: help desk, junior admin, basic network checks. The firms near me will need fewer juniors, and I'd be at the back of the queue with my pass and no internship. I don't think the whole world ends, but I think my particular path is narrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for work in places that need a person in the room: schools, the parish office, the hospital's on-site IT, the council. I'd take a job with an apprenticeship, even a low-paid one. If I have to, I'd learn the new tools, but I'd ask for training from an employer rather than teach myself. I'd also ask Father Dominic and the parish community whether anyone could take me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit hurt. I've done what I was told: study, work hard, be honest. It feels like the rule changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it feels like the rule changed. Who changed it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, mostly. They pushed this and they'll keep the savings. I'm not against business, I think it's how people get on, but a business should take care of the people who built it, and they're doing the opposite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept help from the government or church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the church, yes, because it's a family. From the government, only if it's a training place or a job, not money for nothing. Dad says a man who's given a handout loses a piece of himself. I half agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is cruel. I'd say it plainly: families aren't ready and neither is the parish. I'd say the government should not let this land on young people without a plan, and that employers should be required to keep trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. If AI can do any thinking work, then I'm the kind of graduate who is replaced first. I finish the master's in a year, and I'd step into nothing. I'd have thirty-two thousand to pay, a pass, no job and no one who can help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for any job with my hands and any job with people: care work, the church hall, the school kitchen with my mum. I'd stop the master's if a job turned up. I'd cut everything: no bus pass, no phone contract, no new clothes. I'd lean on my parents for food and the parish for support. And I'd vote and campaign for any politician who put apprenticeships first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd pray a lot. I'd also feel angry, which I don't enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on your parents. What would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say, 'This family has been through worse, and you'll eat at our table.' Mum would cry and then make a pie. They would never complain, but I'd know what it costs them, and that's the hardest part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider moving to find work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it was the last option. I don't want to leave my parents, and I don't know anyone in the city. But if a job came up two hours away, I'd take it and send money home.

I'd say employers should be required to keep trainees.
think: If AI does any thinking work, I'm the kind of graduate who is **replaced first**.

fieldNote: Her **faith and family** are her safety net, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to prepare if people are honest about it. I'd say schools should teach trades and trust alongside screens, and that employers should be encouraged to train young people. I'd say it at church, and I'd say we should look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried but not hopeless. If I get a first job within a year, I'd have years to build something steady. I'd aim at jobs that need a person on site: network cabling, hospital systems. They last longer. But the fear remains that I won't get the first one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and take any paid IT job, even in a small firm. I'd save 100 a month, pay the smaller loan first, and learn network cabling, which works well alongside my degree. I'd ask the council about an apprenticeship scheme. And I'd keep up the church and the youth club, because they keep me steady. I still wouldn't use the AI tools unless the employer insisted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the two-year version, but I'd still wake at four with the numbers in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI tools only if the employer insisted. Why hold back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to know how things work. If a machine writes the network setup and something fails at night, I want to be the person who can fix it. I'd rather be slow and know it than fast and lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they've done their part, and I'll do mine. Dad doesn't read about AI at all. He'd ask me if the church roof needs fixing before it rains, and that's his way of saying he's worried.

I'd say we should look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is time to prepare, and I'd say so. I'd say young people should learn a trade or a craft as well as a degree, and that families and parishes should help them do it. I'd say it as an encouragement, not a warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy rather than frightened. I'd have time to get a first job, pay down my debt and learn a trade. By 2036 I'd be 34, perhaps married with a child. The worry is that I'm slow to change, and ten years could pass while I wait to be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a job in IT support or networking, and save a deposit for a small house near my parents. I'd train for a trade certificate on the side, like electrical installation. I'd learn the AI tools slowly, one at a time, once a few colleagues had used them for a year. And I'd keep up the church work, because a community is part of a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, but I'd keep it to myself. I don't like to say it out loud in case I jinx it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years could pass while you wait to be sure. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a date in my diary every January, and by that date I'd have tried one new thing. Even if it's just one AI tool for one task. Dad does that with the church boiler, he checks it every autumn whether or not it's broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of life would you picture in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small house, a husband who isn't afraid of work and Sunday lunch with my parents. I'd take a life like that over any amount of clever technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. There's no time to find a job, pay the loan or learn a trade, and young people like me would be the first to go under. What would help is employers taking on trainees, apprenticeships that actually pay, and community support that doesn't treat people as a problem. I'd also ask for the loan not to run like a clock while jobs aren't there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against progress. We just want it to treat people fairly and to remember who's at the bottom of the ladder. I'd take a hard job over a handout every time, but I need someone to offer one.

headlineQuote: I'd take a hard job over a handout every time, but I need someone to offer one.
portrait: Vera is 24, doing a master's in **information systems**, and lives at home with her church-caretaker father and school-cook mother.
She passed her computer science degree with **no internship** and owes about thirty-two thousand.
She's traditional, with free-market and **faith-first** values: work, apprenticeships and family over handouts.
She avoids AI tools, reads notes on paper and wants to **understand** each step of her work.
Her mood is anxious in most scenarios and **alarmed** when the two-year deadline leaves no time to find a first job.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most: no time to find a job, pay the loan or learn a trade.
whatWouldHelp: Employers taking on **trainees**, paid apprenticeships and community support that doesn't treat people as a problem.
A loan that doesn't run like a **clock** while jobs aren't there.
